theme: Truly God is good, Asaph almost slips; then sees the end
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 73. It is the story of a believer who almost lost his faith when he saw the wicked prosper. Notice the turning point in verses 16 and 17.
settingTheScene: Psalm 73 opens Book III of the Psalter and is attributed to Asaph, a Levite who led worship in David’s time. It deals with the problem Job and Ecclesiastes raise: why do the wicked prosper while the righteous suffer? The psalmist tells his own story of almost slipping. It is placed here as the Psalter’s best answer to the Preacher’s puzzles.
observation: “Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart” (v. 1).
“But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped” (v. 2).
“For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (v. 3).
“All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence” (v. 13).
“But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (vv. 16-17).
“I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you” (v. 22).
“Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory” (vv. 23-24).
“Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (vv. 25-26).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a creed: “Truly God is good.” Then the psalmist admits that he almost lost it. He looked at the wicked, who had no pangs and bodies that were fat and sleek, free from trouble, mocking God, and he envied them. He wondered whether his own faithfulness had been pointless. “All in vain have I kept my heart clean.” Many believers have felt this. The Bible lets us say it out loud.

The turning point is a small phrase: “until I went into the sanctuary of God.” The solution to his problem was not a better argument, but worship. In God’s presence, he saw the whole picture: “then I discerned their end.” The wicked are on slippery ground and will be destroyed in a moment. They are like a dream when one awakes. What looked solid is a vapor. Perspective changes everything when we see it from God’s point of view.

The psalmist then confesses how foolish he had been: “I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you.” His envy had been irrational. But he does not stop there. His confession leads to the greatest statement of the psalm: “Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand.” The “nevertheless” is the pivot. Despite his ignorance, God held him. His security rests not on his grip on God but on God’s grip on him.

Verses 25 and 26 are among the most beautiful in the Bible. “Whom have I in heaven but you?” God himself is the treasure. “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” The psalmist ends by saying, “For me it is good to be near God.” This is the answer to the problem of the prosperity of the wicked: God himself is the reward. And with that, the psalmist sees that the wicked, though rich, have nothing.
connection: Jesus said, “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” (Mark 8:36). The sanctuary where the psalmist found perspective is fulfilled in Christ, in whom we have access to God (Hebrews 10:19-22). The poor man Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19-31) illustrate verses 17 to 20. Philippians 3:8 expresses the same treasure: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.”
application:
Think about whom you have envied. Bring it into the sanctuary of God and ask for his perspective.

Pray verses 25 and 26 slowly, and ask whether they are true for you.

When you feel like you are slipping, remember that God holds your right hand.
prayerPrompts: Confess your envy of those who seem to prosper.
Tell him what you see differently in his presence.
Tell him he is the strength of your heart and your portion.
